title: Updating a factorization as the data change
text:
Suppose a design has already been factorized and a small batch of observations arrives. Recomputing the factorization discards the previous work. qrupdate() and qrdowndate() instead modify the existing factors. The corresponding rupdate() and rdowndate() routines retain only the triangular factor.

1 Insert and remove observations
We use full factors as inputs to the QR update routines in these examples. A batch containing \(m\) new rows is supplied as a \(p\times m\) matrix U: its transpose is appended to the design. The position k is one-based; k = n + 1 appends observations.
set.seed(2027)
n <- 120L
p <- 6L
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
initial <- fastQR::qr(X, complete = TRUE)
U <- matrix(rnorm(p * 3L), p, 3L)
X_added <- rbind(X, t(U))
added <- fastQR::qrupdate(
  Q = initial$Q, R = initial$R, k = n + 1L, U = U,
  type = "row", fast = FALSE, complete = TRUE)
removed <- fastQR::qrdowndate(
  Q = added$Q, R = added$R, k = n + 1L, m = ncol(U),
  type = "row", fast = FALSE, complete = TRUE)
relative_error <- function(a, b) {
  norm(as.matrix(a - b), "F") / max(norm(as.matrix(b), "F"), .Machine$double.eps)
}
row_checks <- c(
  after_insertion = relative_error(added$Q %*% added$R, X_added),
  after_deletion = relative_error(removed$Q %*% removed$R, X))
knitr::kable(data.frame(operation = names(row_checks), error = row_checks),
             digits = 16, row.names = FALSE)



operation
error




after_insertion
4e-16


after_deletion
5e-16



stopifnot(max(row_checks) < 1e-10)
Removing the same rows restores the original design, but need not restore identical factor entries. The product is the relevant check. Before downdating, ensure that the remaining design still has full column rank.


2 Insert and remove predictors
For columns, U has the same number of rows as the design. Here two new predictors are inserted before column 3 and then removed from those same positions.
V <- matrix(rnorm(n * 2L), n, 2L)
k <- 3L
X_wider <- cbind(X[, 1:2, drop = FALSE], V, X[, 3:p, drop = FALSE])
wider <- fastQR::qrupdate(
  initial$Q, initial$R, k = k, U = V, type = "column",
  fast = FALSE, complete = TRUE)
narrower <- fastQR::qrdowndate(
  wider$Q, wider$R, k = k, m = ncol(V), type = "column",
  fast = FALSE, complete = TRUE)
stopifnot(relative_error(wider$Q %*% wider$R, X_wider) < 1e-10,
          relative_error(narrower$Q %*% narrower$R, X) < 1e-10)


3 Update only the triangular factor
For new rows, the Gram identity becomes \[
X_{\mathrm{new}}^\top X_{\mathrm{new}}=X^\top X+UU^\top
=R^\top R+UU^\top.
\] rupdate() returns a new triangular factor satisfying this identity, without returning \(Q\). To delete those rows, rdowndate() takes their values in U rather than their positions.
R_initial <- initial$R[seq_len(p), , drop = FALSE]
R_added <- fastQR::rupdate(X, R_initial, U = U, type = "row", fast = FALSE)
R_removed <- fastQR::rdowndate(R_added, U = U, type = "row", fast = FALSE)

# R-only column updates append new columns to the right.
R_wider <- fastQR::rupdate(X, R_initial, U = V, type = "column", fast = FALSE)
R_narrower <- fastQR::rdowndate(R_wider, k = p + 1L, m = ncol(V),
                               type = "column", fast = FALSE)
r_checks <- c(
  add_rows = relative_error(crossprod(R_added), crossprod(X_added)),
  remove_rows = relative_error(crossprod(R_removed), crossprod(X)),
  add_columns = relative_error(crossprod(R_wider), crossprod(cbind(X, V))),
  remove_columns = relative_error(crossprod(R_narrower), crossprod(X)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(operation = names(r_checks), error = r_checks),
             digits = 16, row.names = FALSE)



operation
error




add_rows
3e-16


remove_rows
2e-16


add_columns
2e-16


remove_columns
2e-16



stopifnot(max(r_checks) < 1e-10)


4 A sliding-window regression
A moving window provides a statistical example of repeated updating and downdating. At each step we discard the oldest observation and append a new one. In addition to \(R\), we maintain \(h=X^\top y\). The regression coefficient vector solves \[
R^\top z=h,\qquad R\widehat\beta=z.
\] Both triangular solves are needed; solving only \(R\widehat\beta=h\) does not solve the normal equations.
The simulation below keeps 100 observations in the window and processes 30 replacements. An intercept is included explicitly. At every step we compare the updated solution with a fresh lm.fit() fit.
set.seed(2028)
window <- 100L
steps <- 30L
p <- 5L
X_stream <- cbind(1, matrix(rnorm((window + steps) * (p - 1L)),
                            window + steps, p - 1L))
beta_true <- c(1, 2, -1, 0, .5)
y_stream <- drop(X_stream %*% beta_true + rnorm(window + steps, sd = .7))
X_window <- X_stream[seq_len(window), , drop = FALSE]
y_window <- y_stream[seq_len(window)]
R_window <- fastQR::qr(X_window, complete = FALSE)$R
h <- crossprod(X_window, y_window)
coef_update <- coef_fresh <- matrix(NA_real_, steps, p)
gram_error <- numeric(steps)
for (s in seq_len(steps)) {
  old_x <- X_window[1, , drop = FALSE]
  old_y <- y_window[1]
  new_x <- X_stream[window + s, , drop = FALSE]
  new_y <- y_stream[window + s]
  R_minus <- fastQR::rdowndate(R_window, U = t(old_x), type = "row")
  X_minus <- X_window[-1, , drop = FALSE]
  R_window <- fastQR::rupdate(X_minus, R_minus, U = t(new_x), type = "row")
  h <- h - crossprod(old_x, old_y) + crossprod(new_x, new_y)
  X_window <- rbind(X_minus, new_x)
  y_window <- c(y_window[-1], new_y)
  coef_update[s, ] <- backsolve(R_window, forwardsolve(t(R_window), h))
  coef_fresh[s, ] <- lm.fit(X_window, y_window)$coefficients
  gram_error[s] <- relative_error(crossprod(R_window), crossprod(X_window))
}
max_coefficient_error <- max(abs(coef_update - coef_fresh))
stopifnot(max_coefficient_error < 1e-9, max(gram_error) < 1e-10)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  check = c("Maximum coefficient difference", "Maximum relative Gram error"),
  value = c(max_coefficient_error, max(gram_error))), digits = 16)



check
value




Maximum coefficient difference
5.81e-14


Maximum relative Gram error
2.04e-14



path_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(step = rep(seq_len(steps), p), coefficient = factor(rep(seq_len(p), each = steps)),
             estimate = as.vector(coef_update), method = "Updated factors"),
  data.frame(step = rep(seq_len(steps), p), coefficient = factor(rep(seq_len(p), each = steps)),
             estimate = as.vector(coef_fresh), method = "Fresh fit"))
ggplot2::ggplot(path_data, ggplot2::aes(step, estimate, colour = coefficient,
                                      linetype = method)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = .8) +
  ggplot2::scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Fresh fit" = "dashed", "Updated factors" = "solid")) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Window replacement", y = "Coefficient estimate", colour = "Coefficient",
                linetype = NULL) + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)



Coefficient estimates as the window advances. Solid lines use updated factors; dashed lines are fresh least-squares fits. The two computations agree to numerical precision.


This example illustrates the algorithm, not a claim about universal speed or long-run stability. Over long sequences, monitor reconstruction or Gram errors and consider periodic refactorization. Maintaining only \(R\) avoids storing \(Q\), but this particular example retains the data window so that observations can be deleted and reference fits checked.

title: Least squares, ridge paths and model selection
text:
This chapter connects the factorizations to statistical estimates. The examples use type = "QR" and check the coefficient vectors against independent reference calculations. Matrix inputs do not automatically encode a formula: an intercept must be supplied or handled by centering.

1 Least squares with predictions
We generate six predictors, of which three have nonzero coefficients, and an intercept. The test observations are generated independently of the training observations.
set.seed(2029)
n <- 160L
p <- 6L
n_test <- 400L
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
X_test <- matrix(rnorm(n_test * p), n_test, p)
beta_true <- c(2, -1.5, .75, 0, 0, 0)
y <- drop(1 + X %*% beta_true + rnorm(n, sd = 1.5))
y_test <- drop(1 + X_test %*% beta_true + rnorm(n_test, sd = 1.5))
design <- cbind(intercept = 1, X)
design_test <- cbind(intercept = 1, X_test)
ols <- fastQR::qrls(y, design, X_test = design_test, type = "QR")
stopifnot(max(abs(ols$coeff - lm.fit(design, y)$coefficients)) < 1e-10)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  term = c("Intercept", paste0("x", seq_len(p))),
  truth = c(1, beta_true), estimate = as.numeric(ols$coeff)), digits = 4)

ols_test_mse <- mean((y_test - drop(design_test %*% ols$coeff))^2)
ols_test_mse
## [1] 2.238406
The error on the independent test set estimates predictive performance; it is not the training residual variance. We compute the squared residual loss explicitly from predictions so that the quantity being reported is unambiguous.
ggplot2::ggplot(data.frame(observed = y_test,
                          predicted = drop(design_test %*% ols$coeff)),
                ggplot2::aes(observed, predicted)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = .4, colour = "#b5121b") +
  ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "#526070") +
  ggplot2::coord_equal() + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)



Independent test responses versus least-squares predictions. The diagonal is a reference line, not a fitted trend.




2 Ridge: scaling the penalty and handling the intercept
For qrridge(..., type = "QR"), the coefficient vector solves \[
\widehat\beta_\lambda
=\arg\min_b\left\{\frac{1}{n}\|y-Xb\|_2^2+\lambda\|b\|_2^2\right\}
=(X^\top X+n\lambda I_p)^{-1}X^\top y.
\] Here lambda is a scalar. We build a path by calling the function once per grid value. All supplied columns are penalized. To leave the intercept unpenalized, center the response and predictors, estimate the slopes, and reconstruct the intercept. We also scale predictors using training-set standard deviations so that a common penalty has a comparable interpretation across columns.
x_mean <- colMeans(X)
x_scale <- apply(X, 2, sd)
y_mean <- mean(y)
Z <- sweep(sweep(X, 2, x_mean, "-"), 2, x_scale, "/")
y_centered <- y - y_mean
lambda <- exp(seq(log(1e-4), log(10), length.out = 50L))
path_standardized <- vapply(lambda, function(lam) {
  as.numeric(fastQR::qrridge(y_centered, Z, lambda = lam, type = "QR")$coeff)
}, numeric(p))
path_slopes <- sweep(path_standardized, 1, x_scale, "/")
path_intercept <- y_mean - drop(crossprod(x_mean, path_slopes))

# Independent augmented-design QR calculation at one grid value.
j <- 20L
reference <- qr.coef(base::qr(rbind(Z, sqrt(n * lambda[j]) * diag(p))),
                     c(y_centered, rep(0, p)))
stopifnot(max(abs(path_standardized[, j] - reference)) < 1e-10)
path_table <- data.frame(lambda = rep(lambda, each = p),
                         coefficient = factor(rep(seq_len(p), length(lambda))),
                         estimate = as.vector(path_slopes))
ggplot2::ggplot(path_table, ggplot2::aes(lambda, estimate, colour = coefficient)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = .8) + ggplot2::scale_x_log10() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = expression(lambda), y = "Coefficient estimate", colour = "Predictor") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)



Ridge slopes on their original predictor scale, plotted against a logarithmic penalty grid. Coefficients shrink continuously; ridge does not generally create an exactly sparse fit.




3 Cross-validation with preprocessing inside each fold
We use an explicit five-fold loop around qrridge(..., type = "QR"). This exposes the loss, the penalty normalization and the preprocessing used in each fit. The fold assignment is fixed across the entire grid. Means and scales are estimated using only the training portion of each fold, avoiding information leakage from validation observations.
set.seed(2030)
K <- 5L
fold <- sample(rep(seq_len(K), length.out = n))
squared_error <- matrix(NA_real_, n, length(lambda))
for (k in seq_len(K)) {
  train <- fold != k
  valid <- !train
  mu <- colMeans(X[train, , drop = FALSE])
  sc <- apply(X[train, , drop = FALSE], 2, sd)
  ybar <- mean(y[train])
  Z_train <- sweep(sweep(X[train, , drop = FALSE], 2, mu, "-"), 2, sc, "/")
  Z_valid <- sweep(sweep(X[valid, , drop = FALSE], 2, mu, "-"), 2, sc, "/")
  for (j in seq_along(lambda)) {
    b <- fastQR::qrridge(y[train] - ybar, Z_train,
                         lambda = lambda[j], type = "QR")$coeff
    prediction <- ybar + drop(Z_valid %*% b)
    squared_error[valid, j] <- (y[valid] - prediction)^2
  }
}
cv_mse <- colMeans(squared_error)
best <- which.min(cv_mse)
lambda_selected <- lambda[best]
selected_prediction <- path_intercept[best] + drop(X_test %*% path_slopes[, best])
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  method = c("Least squares", "CV-selected ridge"),
  test_MSE = c(ols_test_mse, mean((y_test - selected_prediction)^2))), digits = 4)



method
test_MSE




Least squares
2.2384


CV-selected ridge
2.2378



lambda_selected
## [1] 0.001676833
The test responses are used only after selection. A single simulation need not favor ridge over least squares. Cross-validation chooses among the candidate penalties; it does not guarantee that the selected fit outperforms every alternative on new data. If the selected value lies at a grid endpoint, consider extending the grid.
ggplot2::ggplot(data.frame(lambda, MSE = cv_mse), ggplot2::aes(lambda, MSE)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = "#b5121b", linewidth = .9) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = lambda_selected, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#526070") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_log10() + ggplot2::labs(x = expression(lambda), y = "Cross-validated MSE") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)



Validation mean squared error along the penalty grid. The dashed line marks the minimum on this grid.




4 Effective degrees of freedom along the ridge path
For a fixed design, fixed preprocessing and fixed \(\lambda\), ridge is linear in \(y\). If \(d_j\) are the singular values of the centered, standardized design \(Z\), the effective degrees of freedom including the unpenalized intercept are \[
\mathrm{df}(\lambda)=1+\sum_{j=1}^p\frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2+n\lambda}.
\] This calculation is provided explicitly in the tutorial; it is not taken from the package’s returned df field. It describes each fixed-penalty candidate, not the additional complexity of selecting \(\lambda\) using the responses.
d2 <- svd(Z, nu = 0, nv = 0)$d^2
df_path <- vapply(lambda, function(lam) 1 + sum(d2 / (d2 + n * lam)), numeric(1))
stopifnot(all(diff(df_path) <= 0), all(df_path >= 1), all(df_path <= p + 1))
ggplot2::ggplot(data.frame(lambda, df = df_path), ggplot2::aes(lambda, df)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = "#b5121b", linewidth = .9) + ggplot2::scale_x_log10() +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = lambda_selected, linetype = "dashed") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = expression(lambda), y = "Effective degrees of freedom") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)



Effective degrees of freedom for each fixed ridge penalty, including the unpenalized intercept.




5 Multiple responses
When several outcomes share a design, qrmls() estimates a coefficient matrix. The same factorization can be reused across outcomes. Here we check its result against a base-R QR least-squares calculation.
set.seed(2031)
Y <- cbind(y, drop(-.5 + X %*% c(0, 1, 0, -1, 0, .5) + rnorm(n)))
multivariate <- fastQR::qrmls(Y, design, type = "QR")
reference <- qr.coef(base::qr(design), Y)
stopifnot(max(abs(multivariate$coeff - reference)) < 1e-10)
knitr::kable(as.matrix(multivariate$coeff), digits = 4,
             col.names = c("Response 1", "Response 2"))

max(abs(factorization$Q %*% factorization$R - X))

title: Numerical accuracy and reproducible timing
text:
A useful comparison asks two questions: are the defining identities satisfied, and how much work is needed to obtain the required representation? Compact factors, explicit thin factors and full factors are different outputs and should not be pooled into a single speed ranking.

1 Accuracy as the condition number increases
We construct designs with prescribed singular values. The exact coefficient vector is known, and the response is formed without additional noise. Reconstruction error measures how accurately the factors represent the design; coefficient error measures the accuracy of a subsequent least-squares solve. These quantities can behave differently as conditioning deteriorates.
set.seed(2032)
n <- 160L
p <- 12L
U <- qr.Q(base::qr(matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)))
V <- qr.Q(base::qr(matrix(rnorm(p * p), p, p)))
beta <- seq(-1, 1, length.out = p)
condition_numbers <- 10^(0:8)
accuracy <- do.call(rbind, lapply(condition_numbers, function(kappa_target) {
  singular_values <- exp(seq(0, -log(kappa_target), length.out = p))
  X <- sweep(U, 2, singular_values, "*") %*% t(V)
  y <- drop(X %*% beta)
  f <- fastQR::qr(X, complete = FALSE)
  b_qr <- backsolve(f$R, crossprod(f$Q, y))
  b_normal <- tryCatch(solve(crossprod(X), crossprod(X, y)),
                        error = function(e) rep(NA_real_, p))
  data.frame(condition = kappa_target,
    reconstruction = norm(X - f$Q %*% f$R, "F") / norm(X, "F"),
    QR_coefficients = sqrt(sum((b_qr - beta)^2) / sum(beta^2)),
    normal_equations = sqrt(sum((b_normal - beta)^2) / sum(beta^2)))
}))

ggplot2::ggplot(accuracy_long, ggplot2::aes(condition, pmax(error, .Machine$double.eps), colour = metric)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(na.rm = TRUE) + ggplot2::geom_point(na.rm = TRUE) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_log10() + ggplot2::scale_y_log10() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = expression(kappa[2](X)), y = "Relative error", colour = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")



Relative reconstruction and coefficient errors versus the prescribed condition number. Missing normal-equation values indicate that the reference solver rejected the system as numerically singular.


Forming \(X^\top X\) squares the spectral condition number. A small QR reconstruction error does not imply that every downstream algorithm is equally stable. In particular, this comparison uses an explicit triangular QR solve and is not a stability claim about every regression wrapper in the package. Errors below machine epsilon are plotted at epsilon for readability.


2 Timing a row update against refactorization
We compare two ways to obtain a triangular factor for the same enlarged matrix: updating an existing \(R\), and computing a fresh thin QR factorization. The initial factorization is excluded from the update timing because this is the situation in which factors are already available. The fresh calculation also produces \(Q\); a separate rchol() comparison provides an R-only refactorization baseline.
We use three design sizes, ten new rows, five repetitions, warm-up calls and adaptively sized batches to reduce clock-resolution effects. Random-data generation, correctness checks and plotting are excluded from timed regions. The reported times are seconds per call, not elapsed time for an entire batch.
set.seed(2033)
repetitions <- 5L
sizes <- c(500L, 1000L, 2000L)
p <- 40L
m <- 10L
elapsed_per_call <- function(fun, batch_size) {
  unname(system.time(for (i in seq_len(batch_size)) fun())["elapsed"]) / batch_size
}
timing <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sizes, function(n) {
  X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
  U <- matrix(rnorm(p * m), p, m)
  X_new <- rbind(X, t(U))
  R <- fastQR::qr(X, complete = FALSE)$R
  methods <- list(
    "R update" = function() fastQR::rupdate(X, R, U, type = "row", fast = FALSE),
    "Fresh thin QR" = function() fastQR::qr(X_new, complete = FALSE),
    "Fresh R only" = function() fastQR::rchol(X_new))
  updated <- methods[[1]]()
  gram_error <- norm(crossprod(updated) - crossprod(X_new), "F") / norm(crossprod(X_new), "F")
  stopifnot(gram_error < 1e-10)
  invisible(lapply(methods, function(fun) fun()))
  batches <- vapply(methods, function(fun) {
    b <- 1L
    repeat {
      elapsed <- unname(system.time(for (i in seq_len(b)) fun())["elapsed"])
      if (elapsed >= .05 || b >= 4096L) break
      b <- b * 2L
    }
    b
  }, integer(1))
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(repetitions), function(rep) {
    # Randomize execution order within each repetition.
    order <- sample(names(methods))
    data.frame(n = n, p = p, added_rows = m, repetition = rep, method = order,
      batch_calls = unname(batches[order]),
      seconds = vapply(order, function(name)
        elapsed_per_call(methods[[name]], batches[[name]]), numeric(1)))
  }))
}))
timing_summary <- aggregate(seconds ~ n + method, timing, median)

             col.names = c("Original rows", "Method", "Median seconds per call"))

  ggplot2::geom_boxplot(position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = .8), outlier.shape = NA) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = .8), size = 1.6) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_log10() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Original number of observations", y = "Milliseconds per call (log scale)", colour = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")



Measured time to obtain factors after adding ten observations. Initial factors are assumed available for the update. Points and boxes summarize five repetitions; each repetition averages a calibrated batch of calls.


At the largest row count in this run, updating the available factor takes a median of 0.041 milliseconds, compared with 1.11 milliseconds for R-only refactorization. This comparison applies to ten added rows and excludes the initial factorization from the update cost. The fresh thin-QR method also constructs \(Q\), so it answers a more demanding output request.
Timings depend on the machine, BLAS implementation, thread configuration and workload. A value printed as zero is below timer resolution and should not be interpreted as zero computational cost; increase the calibration duration if this occurs. These results illustrate this workload and do not establish a universal speed ranking. The code deliberately keeps input checking enabled.


3 Comparing QR interfaces
This comparison retains the five interfaces of the original benchmark: base::qr, fastQR::qr, fastQR::qr_fast with and without pivoting, and Matrix::qr. These calls return different representations: the timings compare the named interfaces, not identical output objects. The Matrix call below receives an ordinary dense R matrix, as in the original example; it is not a sparse-QR benchmark. Pivoting also performs additional work.
The default settings keep rebuilding this guide practical. Set options(fastQR.guide.full_benchmarks = TRUE) before source("build.R") to use the original large dimension grid and twenty repetitions in the scaling experiments. All displayed tables are generated from the actual settings, without loading historical timing files.
full_benchmarks <- isTRUE(getOption("fastQR.guide.full_benchmarks", FALSE))
benchmark_reps <- if (full_benchmarks) 20L else 5L
benchmark_n <- if (full_benchmarks) 2000L else 500L
benchmark_p <- if (full_benchmarks) c(20L,40L,100L,200L,400L,800L,1200L,1500L,1800L) else c(20L,40L,80L)
measure_methods <- function(methods, repetitions) {
  invisible(lapply(methods, function(f) f()))
  batches <- vapply(methods, function(f) {
    b <- 1L
    repeat {
      seconds <- unname(system.time(for (i in seq_len(b)) f())["elapsed"])
      if (seconds >= .05 || b >= 4096L) break
      b <- b * 2L
    }
    b
  }, integer(1))
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(repetitions), function(rep) {
    order <- sample(names(methods))
    data.frame(repetition = rep, method = order, batch_calls = unname(batches[order]),
      seconds = vapply(order, function(k) elapsed_per_call(methods[[k]], batches[[k]]), numeric(1)))
  }))
}
set.seed(2041)
interface_n <- if (full_benchmarks) 1000L else 300L
interface_p <- if (full_benchmarks) 500L else 60L
interface_reps <- if (full_benchmarks) 10L else 5L
X_interface <- matrix(rnorm(interface_n * interface_p, 1), interface_n, interface_p)
interface_methods <- list(
  "base::qr (compact)" = function() base::qr(X_interface),
  "fastQR::qr (thin)" = function() fastQR::qr(X_interface, nb = 5, complete = FALSE),
  "qr_fast, no pivot" = function() fastQR::qr_fast(X_interface, pivot = FALSE),
  "qr_fast, pivot" = function() fastQR::qr_fast(X_interface, pivot = TRUE),
  "Matrix::qr (dense input)" = function() Matrix::qr(X_interface))
interface_timing <- measure_methods(interface_methods, interface_reps)
knitr::kable(aggregate(seconds ~ method, interface_timing, median), digits = 6,
  caption = sprintf("Median seconds per call: n = %d, p = %d, repetitions = %d.",
                    interface_n, interface_p, interface_reps))

Pivoting can change the algorithm and its cost; a small observed timing difference is not evidence that pivoting is intrinsically free or beneficial.


4 QR, Cholesky and linear-system scaling benchmarks
We retain both block-size choices, \(5\) and \(p/2\), and the three workloads from the original vignette. Within each dimension, every method receives the same data. Input generation, validation and plotting are excluded from the timings; execution order is randomized within each repetition, and calls are batched to reduce clock-resolution effects. Repetitions measure timing variability on a fixed matrix, rather than variation across independently generated problems.

QR decomposition: fastQR::qr returns explicit thin factors, whereas base::qr returns compact factors. The different outputs must be considered when interpreting execution times.
Triangular factor: qrchol(X) is compared with both chol(crossprod(X)), which includes forming the Gram matrix, and chol(G) with \(G=X^\top X\) already available. Keeping both baselines makes the cost of forming \(G\) explicit.
Linear-system solution: both solvers receive the same precomputed \(G=X^\top X\) and \(h=X^\top y\). Thus neither method is charged for forming these inputs. This reproduces the original normal-equation workload; it is not a comparison of direct least-squares solvers acting on \(X\).

set.seed(2042)
benchmark_validation <- list()
scaling_timing <- do.call(rbind, lapply(benchmark_p, function(p) {
  n <- benchmark_n
  X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
  y <- rnorm(n)
  G <- crossprod(X); h <- crossprod(X, y)
  block <- max(1L, p %/% 2L)
  b_reference <- base::qr.solve(G, h)
  errors <- numeric()
  for (nb in c(5L, block)) {
    f <- fastQR::qr(X, nb = nb, complete = FALSE)
    U <- fastQR::qrchol(X, nb = nb)
    b <- fastQR::qrsolve(A = G, b = h, nb = nb)
    errors <- c(errors, norm(X - f$Q %*% f$R, "F") / norm(X, "F"),
      norm(crossprod(U) - G, "F") / norm(G, "F"),
      sqrt(sum((b - b_reference)^2)) / max(1, sqrt(sum(b_reference^2))))
  }
  stopifnot(max(errors) < 1e-8)
  benchmark_validation[[as.character(p)]] <<- data.frame(p = p, max_relative_error = max(errors))
  workloads <- list(
    QR = list("fastQR, nb = 5" = function() fastQR::qr(X, nb = 5, complete = FALSE),
      "fastQR, nb = p/2" = function() fastQR::qr(X, nb = block, complete = FALSE),
      "base QR (compact)" = function() base::qr(X)),
    Cholesky = list("qrchol, nb = 5" = function() fastQR::qrchol(X, nb = 5),
      "qrchol, nb = p/2" = function() fastQR::qrchol(X, nb = block),
      "chol, Gram available" = function() base::chol(G),
      "crossprod + chol" = function() base::chol(crossprod(X))),
    Solve = list("qrsolve, nb = 5" = function() fastQR::qrsolve(G, h, nb = 5),
      "qrsolve, nb = p/2" = function() fastQR::qrsolve(G, h, nb = block),
      "base qr.solve" = function() base::qr.solve(G, h)))
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(workloads), function(workload) {
    out <- measure_methods(workloads[[workload]], benchmark_reps)
    out$workload <- workload; out$n <- n; out$p <- p
    out
  }))
}))

benchmark_plot("Solve")



Solution times for the same precomputed normal-equation system.


At the largest tested dimension (p = 80), the smallest median time is 0.107 milliseconds per call for base qr.solve. Both solvers start from the same precomputed normal-equation system. The differences therefore concern the solution stage, not preprocessing or prediction. The validation table checks agreement separately from execution time; a faster call would not be useful if it failed that check.
The normal-equation workload squares the condition number of the design, as discussed above. Good agreement on these random examples does not remove that limitation. The supplied large-grid option can be computationally expensive; the small default run supplies reproducible examples, not evidence of performance at untested dimensions. No historical cached measurements are mixed with these newly computed results.

title: From a matrix to a verified QR factorization
text:
A QR factorization is a reusable numerical representation of a design matrix. It is useful both for solving a single least-squares problem and for updating that solution as observations or predictors change. This tutorial starts with the factorization itself, then follows those changes through worked statistical examples.
The examples use fastQR 1.1.5, ggplot2 for figures and knitr for tables. All code uses explicit fastQR:: or base:: namespaces because both packages export a function named qr. Install the released package with install.packages("fastQR"); no attachment with library(fastQR) is required below.

1 Full, thin and compact representations
Let \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) have full column rank, with \(n>p\). Its thin factorization is \[
X=Q_1R_1,\qquad Q_1^\top Q_1=I_p,
\] where \(Q_1\) is \(n\times p\) and \(R_1\) is nonsingular, upper triangular and \(p\times p\). The columns of \(Q_1\) are orthonormal; \(Q_1Q_1^\top\) is a projector and need not equal \(I_n\).
The full factorization completes \(Q_1\) to an orthogonal matrix by adding \(n-p\) orthonormal columns: \[
\begin{aligned}
Q&=[Q_1,Q_2]\in\mathbb R^{n\times n},
& Q_2&\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-p)},\\
R&=\begin{pmatrix}R_1\\0_{(n-p)\times p}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{n\times p},
& X&=QR=Q_1R_1.
\end{aligned}
\] Here \(Q_1^\top Q_2=0_{p\times(n-p)}\) and \(Q_2^\top Q_2=I_{n-p}\), so \(Q_2\) spans the orthogonal complement of the column space of \(X\). The zero block in \(R\) contributes nothing to the product; the thin representation therefore suffices to reconstruct \(X\).
An upper triangular \(R_1\) is not generally symmetric or positive definite: it is \(R_1^\top R_1=X^\top X\) that is positive definite.

2 A first reproducible example
We generate a modest, full-rank design so that the dimensions and checks are easy to inspect. complete = FALSE avoids constructing an unnecessary \(n\times n\) matrix.
set.seed(2026)
n <- 120L
p <- 6L
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
thin <- fastQR::qr(X, type = "householder", complete = FALSE)
full <- fastQR::qr(X, type = "householder", complete = TRUE)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  representation = c("Thin", "Full"),
  Q_rows = c(nrow(thin$Q), nrow(full$Q)),
  Q_columns = c(ncol(thin$Q), ncol(full$Q)),
  R_rows = c(nrow(thin$R), nrow(full$R)),

The following helper measures error relative to the size of the reference matrix, using the Frobenius norm. It will also be used in the update examples.
relative_error <- function(actual, reference) {
  norm(as.matrix(actual - reference), "F") /
    max(norm(as.matrix(reference), "F"), .Machine$double.eps)
}
checks <- c(
  thin_reconstruction = relative_error(thin$Q %*% thin$R, X),
  full_reconstruction = relative_error(full$Q %*% full$R, X),
  thin_orthogonality = relative_error(crossprod(thin$Q), diag(p)),
  Gram_identity = relative_error(crossprod(thin$R), crossprod(X)))

These are checks of the defining identities. Comparing two implementations’ entries of \(Q\) and \(R\) directly would be misleading: paired column/row sign changes can produce equally valid factors.


3 Pivoting: keep track of the column order
Column pivoting changes the order in which the columns are factorized. With the permutation matrix returned by qr_pivot2perm(), the convention used here is \[
X=QRP,\qquad XP^\top=QR.
\] Thus the correct Gram check is \(R^\top R=PX^\top XP^\top\), not generally \(R^\top R=X^\top X\).
packed <- fastQR::qr_fast(X, pivot = TRUE)
Q <- fastQR::qr_Q(packed$qr, tau = packed$qraux,
                  rank = packed$rank, complete = FALSE)
R <- fastQR::qr_R(packed$qr, rank = NULL, complete = FALSE)
P <- fastQR::qr_pivot2perm(packed$pivot)
pivot_checks <- c(
  reconstruction = relative_error(Q %*% R %*% P, X),
  permuted_Gram = relative_error(crossprod(R), crossprod(X %*% t(P))))
knitr::kable(data.frame(check = names(pivot_checks), error = pivot_checks),
             digits = 16, row.names = FALSE)

All subsequent update examples start from unpivoted factors, so that insertion and deletion positions refer directly to the original columns. Rank-deficient designs require additional care; the worked examples retain full column rank.


4 Triangular factors and linear systems
When only the Gram factor is needed, storing \(Q\) may be unnecessary. The two functions below return triangular factors; we check the invariant rather than their signs.
R_qr <- fastQR::qrchol(X)
R_only <- fastQR::rchol(X)
stopifnot(relative_error(crossprod(R_qr), crossprod(X)) < 1e-10,
          relative_error(crossprod(R_only), crossprod(X)) < 1e-10)

A <- crossprod(X) + diag(p)
b <- seq_len(p)
solution <- fastQR::qrsolve(A, b, type = "QR")
relative_error(A %*% solution, b)
## [1] 6.092069e-16
stopifnot(relative_error(A %*% solution, b) < 1e-10)
The square system above is deliberately well conditioned. Later examples distinguish factorization error from the sensitivity of a least-squares solution to an ill-conditioned design.

3.1 Scope of the regression examples
The worked ridge and CV examples use qrridge(..., type = "QR") with an explicit fold loop. That loop makes training-fold scaling and the normalized penalty visible and reproducible. The native CV routines, the ridge type = "R" route and the multiple-response ridge routines are not validated recommendations in this guide. In particular, numerical checks of the first two uncovered discrepancies requiring a separate implementation review.

title: Mathematical background and further reading
text:
The computational ideas in this guide build on standard orthogonal factorizations and their modification after changes to a matrix. For full treatments, see Golub and Van Loan (2013) and Björck (2015); for least-squares algorithms, see Björck (2024). The package authors develop updating methods and statistical applications in Bernardi, Busatto, and Cattelan (2024).

1 Why orthogonal transformations?
Multiplication by a square orthogonal matrix preserves the Euclidean norm. If \(X=Q_1R_1\) and \(Q=[Q_1,Q_2]\) is a full orthogonal completion, then \[
\|y-Xb\|_2^2
=\|Q_1^\top y-R_1b\|_2^2+\|Q_2^\top y\|_2^2.
\] The second term does not depend on \(b\). For a full-rank design, the least-squares solution is obtained by solving \(R_1\widehat\beta=Q_1^\top y\). This avoids explicitly inverting a matrix.


2 Classical and modified Gram–Schmidt
Let \(X=[x_1,\ldots,x_p]\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) have linearly independent columns, with \(n\geq p\). Classical Gram–Schmidt constructs an orthonormal basis for their span. At step \(k\), set \[
\begin{aligned}
r_{jk}&=q_j^\top x_k\quad(j<k),\\
v_k&=x_k-\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}r_{jk}q_j,\\
r_{kk}&=\|v_k\|_2,\qquad q_k=v_k/r_{kk}.
\end{aligned}
\] The empty sum at \(k=1\) is zero. Full column rank ensures \(r_{kk}>0\) in exact arithmetic. With \(r_{jk}=0\) for \(j>k\), these identities give \(X=QR\) and \(Q^\top Q=I_p\). The temporary residual \(v_k\) is distinct from the normalized vector \(q_k\).
Modified Gram–Schmidt instead starts with \(v=x_k\) and, for \(j=1,\ldots,k-1\), successively computes \[
r_{jk}=q_j^\top v,\qquad v\leftarrow v-r_{jk}q_j;
\] it then sets \(r_{kk}=\|v\|_2\) and \(q_k=v/r_{kk}\). The two algorithms are equivalent in exact arithmetic, but their floating-point behavior differs: computing projections from the updated residual generally reduces loss of orthogonality. Reorthogonalization may still be needed for difficult problems (Golub and Van Loan 2013; Björck 2015).
The following educational implementation checks both defining identities on a well-conditioned example; it is not a replacement for the package’s factorization routines.
mgs <- function(X) {
  n <- nrow(X); p <- ncol(X)
  Q <- matrix(0, n, p); R <- matrix(0, p, p)
  for (k in seq_len(p)) {
    v <- X[, k]
    if (k > 1L) for (j in seq_len(k - 1L)) {
      R[j, k] <- sum(Q[, j] * v)
      v <- v - R[j, k] * Q[, j]
    }
    R[k, k] <- sqrt(sum(v^2))
    if (R[k, k] <= .Machine$double.eps * sqrt(sum(X[, k]^2)))
      stop("Numerically dependent column: use a rank-revealing factorization.")
    Q[, k] <- v / R[k, k]
  }
  list(Q = Q, R = R)
}
set.seed(2040)
X_gs <- matrix(rnorm(80 * 8), 80, 8)
gs <- mgs(X_gs)
gs_checks <- c(reconstruction = norm(X_gs - gs$Q %*% gs$R, "F") / norm(X_gs, "F"),
               orthogonality = norm(crossprod(gs$Q) - diag(8), "F"))
gs_checks
## reconstruction  orthogonality 
##   1.154784e-16   1.019128e-15
stopifnot(max(gs_checks) < 1e-10)


3 Householder transformations and Givens rotations
A Householder reflector has the form \[
H=I-2vv^\top/(v^\top v),\qquad v\ne0.
\] It is symmetric and orthogonal and can eliminate all entries below a selected diagonal entry in a column. A sequence of reflectors produces an upper triangular factor. Compact storage keeps the information defining these reflectors instead of storing every entry of \(Q\).
A Givens rotation acts on two coordinates through the block \[
\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-s&c\end{pmatrix},\qquad c^2+s^2=1.
\] Choosing \(c=a/\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) and \(s=b/\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) maps \((a,b)^\top\) to \((\sqrt{a^2+b^2},0)^\top\) when \((a,b)\ne(0,0)\). Rotations can restore triangular structure after localized changes. Both algorithms exploit orthogonal transformations; neither makes an ill-conditioned statistical problem intrinsically well conditioned.


4 What a row update changes
Write a batch of new observations as \(U^\top\), with \(U\in\mathbb R^{p\times m}\). Starting with \(X=Q_1R_1\), a triangular factor for the enlarged design can be obtained by triangularizing \[
\begin{pmatrix}R_1\\U^\top\end{pmatrix}.
\] The stacked matrix has \(p+m\) rows and \(p\) columns: \(R_1\) is \(p\times p\) and \(U^\top\) is \(m\times p\). Its Gram matrix is \(R_1^\top R_1+UU^\top=X_{\mathrm{new}}^\top X_{\mathrm{new}}\). This explains why the previous triangular factor contains useful information for a row update.
Deleting rows changes the plus sign to a minus sign. A valid downdate requires the remaining design to retain the rank needed by the subsequent solve. The algebraic relation alone does not guarantee favorable conditioning after deletion.


5 Ridge as augmented least squares
For the normalized ridge criterion used in the regression chapter, define the augmented response and design by \[
\widetilde y=\begin{pmatrix}y\\0_p\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{n+p},\qquad
\widetilde X=\begin{pmatrix}X\\\sqrt{n\lambda}I_p\end{pmatrix}
\in\mathbb R^{(n+p)\times p}.
\] The \(p\) additional entries of \(\widetilde y\) are zero, and the \(p\) additional rows of \(\widetilde X\) encode the penalty. For \(b\in\mathbb R^p\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|\widetilde y-\widetilde Xb\|_2^2
&=\left\|\begin{pmatrix}y-Xb\\-\sqrt{n\lambda}b\end{pmatrix}\right\|_2^2\\
&=\|y-Xb\|_2^2+n\lambda\|b\|_2^2.
\end{aligned}
\] The augmented formulation is useful as an independent QR reference. It also makes the factor \(n\) explicit: changing the normalization of the loss changes the interpretation of \(\lambda\).
The intercept is handled separately in the ridge tutorial by centering. If a column of ones were simply included in the penalized design, that coefficient would also be penalized. Predictor means and scales must be estimated again within each cross-validation training fold.


6 Choosing a representation
Use compact factors when storage is important and \(Q\) need not be explicitly formed. Use thin factors when orthogonal projections or direct QR solves are needed. Use full factors when an operation requires an orthogonal completion, as in the QR update examples here. An R-only representation is attractive when Gram information and triangular solves suffice, but auxiliary quantities such as \(X^\top y\) still need to be maintained for regression.
The worked examples demonstrate these distinctions through reconstruction identities, independent solutions and measured timings. They should be read together with the function documentation for the installed package version.
